raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) and represents the most important replacement of conventional renin–angiotensin system blockade in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Its rationale arose from two mature therapeutic concepts: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition improves survival in severe and mild-to-moderate systolic heart failure [1,2], and angiotensin receptor blockade provides neurohormonal antagonism when ACE inhibition is insufficient or not tolerated [3]. Neprilysin inhibition augments endogenous natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and other vasoactive peptides, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, antifibrotic signaling, and reverse remodeling. Earlier combined ACE–neprilysin inhibition with omapatrilat was limited by angioedema, attributed to overlapping bradykinin/substance P degradation pathways [4,5]. Sacubitril/valsartan avoided ACE inhibition by pairing the neprilysin prodrug sacubitril with valsartan; phase 2 hypertension data confirmed potent blood-pressure lowering and acceptable tolerability [6].

The pivotal PARADIGM-HF program tested this concept against enalapril, not placebo, in ambulatory symptomatic HFrEF after run-in tolerability assessment [7]. In PARADIGM-HF, sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, all-cause mortality, and sudden and pump-failure deaths compared with enalapril [8,9]. Importantly, benefits were not confined to first events: clinical deterioration, need for treatment intensification, emergency visits, and recurrent hospitalizations were also reduced [10]. The safety profile was distinctive: more symptomatic hypotension but less cough, hyperkalemia, and renal impairment than enalapril in the trial population. Secondary analyses suggested fewer severe hyperkalemia events among patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [11], improved glycemic control in patients with diabetes [12], and slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate despite modest early creatinine changes [13].

Subsequent trials addressed implementation. PIONEER-HF showed that initiating sacubitril/valsartan during hospitalization for acute decompensated HFrEF, once hemodynamically stable, produced greater NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, or angioedema [14]. Its clinical-outcomes analysis, although not powered as a definitive morbidity trial, suggested fewer rehospitalizations [15]. TRANSITION supported either in-hospital or early post-discharge initiation, emphasizing that decongestion, stable blood pressure, and renal/potassium surveillance are more important than waiting for prolonged outpatient stability [16]. TITRATION showed that gradual uptitration can improve attainment of target dose in patients naïve to, or on low doses of, ACE inhibitors/ARBs [17]. Mechanistic studies reinforced biological plausibility: PROVE-HF linked NT-proBNP reduction after initiation to improvements in left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction [18], whereas EVALUATE-HF did not demonstrate a significant reduction in central aortic stiffness versus enalapril over 12 weeks, suggesting that reverse remodeling is not simply explained by large-vessel effects [19].

Evidence in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has been more nuanced. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction with sacubitril/valsartan than valsartan in HFpEF, with signals for left atrial reverse remodeling [20]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested heterogeneity by ejection fraction and sex [21]. Women appeared to derive greater reduction in heart-failure hospitalization than men [22], and pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF supported a gradient of benefit extending into mildly reduced ejection fraction, with attenuation at higher ejection fractions [23]. In contemporary HFpEF care, this positions sacubitril/valsartan as a selective option—particularly for patients with ejection fraction below normal and recurrent congestion—rather than a universal foundational therapy, especially as sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors have shown broader HFpEF outcome benefit [24].

Several practical issues determine safe use. Sacubitril/valsartan should not be combined with an ACE inhibitor; a 36-hour washout is required to reduce angioedema risk. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients with prior angioedema related to ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy. Starting dose should reflect blood pressure, renal function, age, frailty, and previous RAAS-inhibitor exposure, with reassessment of creatinine and potassium after initiation and titration. Hypotension is common but often manageable by adjusting diuretics, nitrates, calcium-channel blockers, or other non–mortality-improving vasodilators before abandoning ARNI therapy.

ARNI therapy may also influence associated phenotypes. In functional mitral regurgitation, sacubitril/valsartan reduced regurgitant volume more than valsartan, plausibly through ventricular reverse remodeling and afterload reduction [25]. After acute myocardial infarction complicated by left ventricular dysfunction or pulmonary congestion, PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce its primary endpoint versus ramipril, although event patterns maintained interest in high-risk post-infarction remodeling [26]. In HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan is now best viewed as one component of rapid, comprehensive disease modification alongside mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [27] and SGLT2 inhibitors [28,29]. Guidelines accordingly recommend replacing ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy with ARNI in eligible symptomatic HFrEF patients and increasingly support early initiation rather than late “step-up” sequencing [30].
